questions.question: A figure is 'embedded' in a host figure when:
options: All its lines appear among the host's lines at the same scale, possibly rotated or reflected
It shares only the outline shape
It is drawn inside a box
questions.rationale: Embedding requires every side of the small figure to lie on lines of the host - at identical scale, with rotation and reflection allowed. A smaller look-alike or a partial match is the standard decoy.

questions.question: The fastest way to search for an embedded figure is to:
options: Anchor on the option's most distinctive feature - longest side, sharpest angle, a dot - and trace from there
Count all lines in the host
questions.rationale: Rare features (dots, arrowheads, double lines, extreme angles) appear in few places, so anchoring on them narrows the search instantly; then trace the shape side by side, verifying each side lands on a host line.

questions.question: While tracing an option figure inside the host, one of its sides floats in blank space. You conclude:
options: The option is not embedded - every side must land on a host line
The option is embedded if the rest matches
questions.rationale: No line may be missing: one floating side disqualifies the option. Distractors are drawn precisely with one invented or missing line - the final verification step catches them.

questions.question: A 2x2 matrix shows circles with one, two and three radial lines in successive cells, the line cluster rotating 45 degrees each step. The fourth cell should contain:
options: Four radial lines at the next 45-degree rotation
Three lines at the original angle
Four lines at the original angle
questions.rationale: Two rules run together: count (+1 line per cell) and rotation (+45 degrees per cell). The correct patch satisfies BOTH - four lines at the next angle. Options fixing one rule while breaking the other are the planted traps.

questions.question: A figure with 180-degree (point) symmetry has one quadrant missing. The correct patch is:
options: The diagonally opposite quadrant rotated 180 degrees
A mirror image of the top quadrant
Any quadrant of the same size
questions.rationale: Point symmetry maps every point through the centre: the missing quadrant must be the given opposite quadrant rotated a half turn. Mirror symmetry would be the rule if the figure reflected across an axis instead.

questions.question: In figure completion, the first step before looking at options should be:
options: State the figure's rules in words (rotation, count, flip, movement)
Guess based on the previous question
questions.rationale: A verbal rule ('arrow rotates 90 clockwise, dot alternates sides') resists the pull of attractive wrong patches. Options are engineered to satisfy exactly one rule - only a complete rule inventory defeats them.

questions.question: A border pattern repeats its design every 4 steps. Given steps 1-3, the figure at step 11 will match:
questions.rationale: Cyclic patterns hide modular arithmetic: 11 mod 4 = 3, so step 11 repeats step 3. Completion questions frequently wrap easy cycle-counting inside pictures.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a standard rule type in figure completion?
questions.rationale: Completion rules operate on elements - rotation, flips, counts, movements, symmetry. Absolute area is not a visual rule examiners use, since figures are printed at fixed size.

questions.question: In a grid completion problem, you must first determine:
options: Whether the rule runs across rows, down columns, or both
The answer to the previous question
questions.rationale: Row-rule and column-rule confusions are deliberate: a cell may fit the row pattern but break the column pattern. Fix the rule's direction before evaluating patches - most wrong answers apply the wrong direction.

questions.question: If an embedded-figure search runs past 90 seconds, the best tactic is:
options: Mark the question and move on - these items are highly time-elastic
questions.rationale: Embedded questions average 30-45 seconds; a 90-second stuck search signals a hidden trick better approached fresh. Bank the easy marks first - the section rewards triage discipline.
